summary:
Forgotten Explorers is an interactive space storytelling web app created for NASA Space Apps’ “Abandoned but Not Forgotten” challenge. It explores the machines left on other worlds, the discoveries they made, and the curiosity that drives exploration.
The final product includes:
- Six rover stories: Apollo 15’s Lunar Roving Vehicle, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity, and Perseverance—with mission photographs, interactive 3D models, and downloadable Blender files.
- A gravity playground: Throw a token and compare how it falls on Earth, Mars, and the Moon.
- “Four Worlds. Countless Questions.”: Explore rotating 3D views of Mercury, Venus, Mars, and the Moon, with longer stories revealed when selected.
- “Beyond the Sun: Stories of Distant Worlds”: Travel from the Solar System to ten exoplanet destinations using a hyperdrive animation, procedural planet visuals, and story panels.
- An animated, responsive interface: Scroll-triggered transitions, space backgrounds, and navigation shortcuts.
- Installable web app support: Add the site to a phone or computer, launch it in its own window, and access cached main pages offline.
The experience combines NASA-based information with creative storytelling and artistic planet reconstructions, making space exploration accessible through interaction.
details:
Forgotten Explorers is an interactive learning app that tells the stories of explorer missions across many worlds, plus the unusual planets beyond them. Each mission is presented as a short story with a 3D simulation, so students experience the mission rather than only reading about it. The app includes a world filter, a motion on/off setting, and a gravity lab where learners drag and release an object on the Moon, Mars and Earth to feel the difference in surface gravity. A special planets section covers ten NASA-discovered planets, and each card separates measured facts from open questions. The app currently includes six explorer stories (Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity and Perseverance) and is free to use in a browser and installable on a phone.

The project aims to help school students and children learn about exploration missions and planets quickly, interactively and memorably. We considered that space learning is often passive, with text, static images and videos, and that ideas like gravity stay abstract for learners. Our approach keeps the scope to explorers on any world a spacecraft has reached, including landers and probes, and treats finished missions as still valuable because of their discoveries. Creativity comes from presenting each explorer by what it taught us, not just its specifications, and from clearly labelling artist illustrations and creative storytelling. Our planned next steps are explorers from other worlds, mission timelines, comparisons, quizzes, and learner testing to measure task completion and gather feedback.
Tools used: Claude, GPT Astra, NASA Space Apps
